name: Monosodium Glutamate
what: The sodium salt of glutamic acid, added to make savoury food taste meatier and more moreish.
why: Generally recognised as safe, but a subset of people get headaches, flushing and sweating after a large dose. It also hides a lot of extra sodium and pushes you to overeat.
adi: No numerical limit set, but keep below about 1 g in a single meal

name: Tartrazine (Yellow 5)
what: A bright lemon-yellow coal-tar dye used in soft drinks, sweets, custard powder and instant noodles.
why: Linked to hyperactivity and reduced attention in children. Also one of the more common triggers of hives and asthma in sensitive people.
adi: 7.5 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Sunset Yellow FCF
what: An orange-yellow azo dye used in orange drinks, snack seasonings and confectionery.
why: One of the Southampton six that European regulators tied to hyperactivity in children. It carries a mandatory warning label across the EU.
adi: 4 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Allura Red AC (Red 40)
what: The most heavily used red dye in the world, found in soft drinks, jelly, sauces, ice cream and candy.
why: Associated with hyperactivity and attention problems in children. Recent animal work also links long-term exposure to gut inflammation.
adi: 7 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Titanium Dioxide
what: A brilliant white mineral pigment used to whiten icing, chewing gum, coffee whiteners and sweets.
why: The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2021 that it can no longer be considered safe, because damage to DNA could not be ruled out. It was banned across the EU in 2022.
adi: No safe level established

name: Sodium Nitrite
what: Keeps cured meat pink and stops botulism in bacon, ham, sausages and salami.
why: Under high heat, and in the stomach, it forms nitrosamines, which are classed as carcinogenic. Processed meat preserved this way is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen.
adi: 0.07 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Sodium Benzoate
what: Stops mould and yeast in acidic products such as soft drinks, pickles, sauces and fruit juice.
why: Safe on its own, but when it sits next to vitamin C in the same bottle it can slowly form benzene, a known carcinogen. Also implicated in child hyperactivity.
effects: Can form benzene with vitamin C
adi: 5 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: TBHQ (Tertiary Butylhydroquinone)
what: A petroleum-derived antioxidant that stops frying oil in chips, noodles and biscuits from going rancid.
why: High doses caused stomach tumours in animal studies, and newer research suggests it can blunt the immune response. Levels in food are low, but they accumulate across a day of packaged snacks.
adi: 0.7 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: BHA (Butylated Hydroxyanisole)
what: A waxy preservative that keeps fats and oils in cereals, chewing gum and instant potato from oxidising.
why: Listed as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen by the US National Toxicology Program, and it behaves as an endocrine disruptor in animal studies.
adi: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: BHT (Butylated Hydroxytoluene)
what: A close cousin of BHA, used in cereals, snack foods and packaging to delay rancidity.
why: Animal studies show liver and thyroid effects at high doses. Evidence in humans is weaker than for BHA, but it is still an avoidable synthetic load.
adi: 0.25 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Aspartame
what: A sweetener roughly 200 times sweeter than sugar, used in diet drinks, sugar-free gum and tabletop sweeteners.
why: Classified in 2023 by IARC as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). Genuinely dangerous for anyone with phenylketonuria, which is why packs carry a phenylalanine warning.
adi: 40 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Acesulfame Potassium
what: A heat-stable sweetener, usually blended with aspartame or sucralose in diet drinks and sugar-free desserts.
why: It passes through the body unchanged, but emerging research points to changes in gut bacteria and to the sweet taste keeping sugar cravings alive.
adi: 9 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Sucralose
what: A chlorinated sugar molecule about 600 times sweeter than sugar, common in diet drinks and no-sugar desserts.
why: Stable and calorie-free, but heating it above 120 C can generate chloropropanols, and studies show it reduces beneficial gut bacteria.
adi: 15 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: High Fructose Corn Syrup
what: A cheap liquid sweetener made by converting corn starch into a fructose-heavy syrup.
why: Fructose is processed almost entirely by the liver. A heavy, regular load drives fatty liver disease, insulin resistance and raised triglycerides, and because it is liquid it does not make you feel full.
adi: No safe regular intake. Count it toward the 25 g daily free-sugar cap

name: Partially Hydrogenated Oil (Trans Fat)
what: Liquid vegetable oil forced solid with hydrogen so it stays cheap, stable and spreadable in bakery goods and fried snacks.
why: The single worst fat in the food supply. It raises LDL cholesterol and lowers HDL at the same time. The WHO has called for total elimination and estimates it causes half a million deaths a year.
adi: Under 1 percent of daily calories, which in practice means avoid entirely

name: Acrylamide
what: Not an added ingredient. It forms by itself when starchy food is fried, roasted or baked above 120 C.
why: Classed by IARC as probably carcinogenic to humans. Levels are highest in deep-fried potato products and over-browned baked goods.
adi: As low as reasonably achievable. No safe threshold is set

name: Palm Oil / Palmolein
what: A cheap, semi-solid tropical oil used in almost every packaged biscuit, spread and instant noodle.
why: About half its fat is saturated, so it pushes up LDL cholesterol. When refined at high temperature it also forms 3-MCPD and glycidyl esters, which EFSA flags as a concern.
adi: Keep total saturated fat under 20 g a day

name: Sulphite Ammonia Caramel
what: The dark brown colour that gives cola, soy sauce and dark bakery goods their shade.
why: Manufacturing it produces 4-methylimidazole, which California lists as a carcinogen and requires a warning label above 29 micrograms per day.
adi: 300 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Phosphoric Acid
what: The sharp tang in cola drinks, also used to stop bacterial growth in fizzy drinks.
why: A high phosphorus load throws off the calcium balance, and cola intake is repeatedly linked to lower bone density. It also erodes tooth enamel directly.
adi: 40 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Potassium Bromate
what: An oxidising agent that makes bread dough rise higher and bake whiter.
why: Classed by IARC as possibly carcinogenic to humans. Residues survive baking when the dough is underproved, which is why most of the world has banned it outright.
adi: No safe level established

name: Sodium Metabisulphite
what: A sulphite that stops dried fruit, packaged juice and pickles from browning and fermenting.
why: A well-documented asthma trigger. Roughly one in twenty asthmatics reacts to sulphites, sometimes severely. It also destroys thiamine, vitamin B1, in the food.
adi: 0.7 mg per kg of body weight per day
restrictedIn: Mandatory allergen declaration above 10 ppm worldwide

name: Disodium Inosinate
what: Almost always paired with MSG, which it makes several times more powerful. Usually derived from meat or fish.
why: It is a purine, so it converts to uric acid in the body, which is a real problem for anyone with gout or kidney stones. Its presence also signals a heavy MSG load.
adi: No numerical limit, but avoid it if you have gout
restrictedIn: Not advised for infants under 12 weeks

name: Maltodextrin
what: A tasteless white starch powder used to bulk out seasoning, sweeteners and instant mixes.
why: Its glycaemic index is higher than table sugar, up to 110, so it spikes blood sugar hard while contributing nothing nutritionally. It also suppresses protective gut bacteria.
adi: No formal limit. Treat it as sugar

name: Carmine (Cochineal)
what: A deep red pigment extracted from crushed cochineal insects, used in yoghurt, juice and confectionery.
why: Not toxic, but it causes genuine anaphylaxis in a small number of people, and it is not vegetarian or vegan despite being labelled a natural colour.
adi: 5 mg per kg of body weight per day
restrictedIn: Mandatory declaration in USA and EU

name: Added Caffeine
what: A stimulant added to energy drinks and colas on top of whatever occurs naturally.
why: Fine in moderation for adults, but easy to overshoot with large energy drinks. It disrupts sleep for up to eight hours and raises heart rate and blood pressure.
adi: 400 mg a day for adults, 100 mg for teenagers, none for children
restrictedIn: Sale to minors restricted in Lithuania, Latvia and Poland

name: Mono- and Diglycerides of Fatty Acids
what: Keeps oil and water mixed in ice cream, bread and margarine so they stay smooth.
why: Considered safe, but it is not covered by trans-fat labelling rules, so partially hydrogenated versions can smuggle small amounts of trans fat into a product declaring zero.
adi: No numerical limit

name: Citric Acid
what: The sour note in citrus fruit, produced industrially and added to almost everything acidic.
why: No health concern at food levels. Frequent contact with the acid can erode tooth enamel over years, which is the only real caveat.
effects: Mild enamel erosion with constant sipping
adi: No limit needed

name: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C)
what: Plain vitamin C, added to stop food browning and to fortify it.
why: Beneficial rather than harmful. The one caution is that it can react with sodium benzoate in the same drink to form benzene.
adi: No limit needed

name: Soy Lecithin
what: A natural fat extracted from soybeans or sunflower seeds that stops chocolate and spreads from separating.
why: No safety concern. Worth knowing about only if you have a soy allergy, since traces of soy protein can carry over.
adi: No limit needed

name: Guar Gum
what: Ground endosperm of the guar bean, used to thicken ice cream, sauces and gluten-free bread.
why: It is soluble fibre, so it is mildly beneficial. Large amounts can cause bloating and gas, but food-level doses will not.
adi: No limit needed

name: Xanthan Gum
what: A fermented sugar-derived gum that gives body to dressings, sauces and gluten-free baking.
why: Safe at food levels and behaves as soluble fibre. Only very large doses have a laxative effect.
adi: No limit needed

name: Potassium Sorbate
what: A mild mould inhibitor used in cheese, baked goods, dried fruit and drinks.
why: One of the gentler preservatives available. Occasional skin or eye irritation is reported, and there is weak evidence of DNA effects in isolated cells at doses far above food levels.
adi: 25 mg per kg of body weight per day

name: Beta-Carotene
what: The orange pigment from carrots, used to colour butter, juice and cheese. The body converts it to vitamin A.
why: Beneficial in food. High-dose supplements are a separate matter and are not advised for smokers, but that does not apply to colouring levels.
adi: No limit needed at colouring levels

name: Malic Acid
what: The tart acid naturally found in apples, added to sour sweets and drinks.
why: No health concern. Like other food acids it can wear tooth enamel if sipped constantly.
effects: Mild enamel erosion with constant sipping
adi: No limit needed
